<b>Altura de la estrella</b><br>Es el án:
Star altitude
It is the angle between the horizon and the star at the moment of recording: 0° on the horizon and 90° right above you (the zenith).

What is it for? Near the horizon the light crosses more air and the measured seeing comes out worse. With the altitude, TurbuLENS also calculates the zenith seeing, which lets you compare different nights and stars: εzenith = ε · (cos z)3/5, with z = 90° − altitude.

How do I get it? In a planetarium program or app (for example Stellarium), with your observing site and the date and time of the recording: look up the star and copy its «altitude». It can be typed with decimals (for example 63.25°).

<b>Calibración de imágenes</b><ul style=:
Image calibration
  • Lights: your sky images (the ones you want to correct).
  • Darks: with the cap on, with the same exposure time, gain and temperature as the lights. They remove dark current and hot pixels.
  • Flats: of an evenly lit surface (twilight sky or a white screen), with the same focus. They correct vignetting and dust.
  • Flat darks (optional): darks with the exposure of the flats.
  • Bias (optional): shortest possible exposure with the cap on. Used if there are no darks.
Each group is combined into a master image (the median is robust to cosmic rays). Then each light is corrected as (light − dark) ÷ normalised flat. Masters and calibrated lights are saved as 32-bit FITS, which DS9, Astropy and AstroImageJ open.
<b>Calibración guiada por las cabeceras<:
Header-guided calibration
Add a whole folder (with subfolders) or single images. TurbuLENS reads the header of each one (FITS, or EXIF for photos) and:
  • Classifies them as lights, darks, flats, flat darks and bias: by the header (IMAGETYP), and if it has none, by the file or folder name. Whatever cannot be told is taken as a light and marked.
  • Matches: each light gets the darks with its same exposure, gain (or ISO), temperature, binning and size, and the flats of its same filter. Flats get their own darks (flat darks).
  • If there are no darks with the same exposure but there is a bias, the dark is scaled: (dark − bias) · tlight / tdark + bias.
Before calibrating you see the plan with its warnings. Each master is created only once and saved as 32-bit FITS («maestros» folder); each light is corrected as (light − dark) ÷ normalised flat («calibradas» folder).
<b>Dark y flat</b><br>Corrigen defectos:
Dark and flat
They correct camera and telescope defects before measuring:

  • Flat: image of a uniform source (twilight sky, white screen). It is divided: it corrects vignetting and dust.
  • Bias: readout with zero exposure. Only needed if you have no dark.
The masters (the combination of many shots) are created in Images mode. They must have the same size as the video (same width and height).

<b>¿Grabaste en video con una cámara de:
Did you record video with a photo camera or a phone?
The camera scales down the sensor image for video: a Nikon D5600 is 6000 pixels wide, but its 1920 px video uses that whole width, so each video pixel covers about 3 sensor pixels.

That is why, for a video, the pixel size that counts is the effective one:
effective pixel = sensor width ÷ video width
(Nikon D5600: 23.5 mm ÷ 1920 px = 12.2 µm, not 3.9 µm).

If you use the sensor pixel, the scale comes out about 3 times too small and the seeing much better than it really is (for example 1″ instead of 3.5″).

Astronomy cameras (QHY, ZWO) record with the real sensor pixels: for them, untick «I recorded video» or choose the camera in the list. The video width is taken from the loaded file.

<b>¿Qué es r?</b><br>El coeficiente de c:
What is r?
Pearson's correlation coefficient (from −1 to 1) tells whether two motions vary together (r > 0), in opposite directions (r < 0) or unrelated (r ≈ 0). The differential motion is split into a longitudinal component (along the line joining the holes) and a transverse one (perpendicular).
  • Longitudinal–transverse r: should be close to 0 (|r| < 0.2). A large |r| reveals something that is not turbulence: vibration or wind in one direction, focus changes or confused spots.
  • r between the two spots: close to 1, common motion dominates (vibration or tracking), which the DIMM cancels; between 0 and 1 is normal; close to 0, each hole sees independent turbulence; negative, focus changes or detection errors.
  • σt/σl: if it is similar to the theoretical √(Kt/Kl), the turbulence behaves as the model predicts.
The PDF report includes this explanation with the values of your analysis.

Cuando tenemos <b>dos variables</b> para:
When we have two variables for each frame, a scatter plot puts one on the x axis and the other on the y axis. The correlation coefficient r goes from −1 to 1:
• r ≈ 1: when one goes up, so does the other;
• r ≈ −1: when one goes up, the other goes down;
• r ≈ 0: there is no linear relationship.

The atmosphere has a short «memory»: one frame resembles the next (high r) but not one half a second later. This shows that turbulence changes within milliseconds.
Cuando una medición depende de muchísimo:
When a measurement depends on a great many small random effects (like thousands of air bubbles), the data usually form a bell: the normal or Gaussian distribution.

The bell is defined only by the mean x̄ and the deviation σ, and follows the 68–95–99.7 rule:
• about 68 % of the data lie within 1 σ of the mean,
• about 95 % within 2 σ,
• almost all (99.7 %) within 3 σ.

Imagina que miras una moneda en el fondo:
Imagine looking at a coin at the bottom of a swimming pool. If the water is still, you see it sharply. If someone stirs the water, the coin trembles and looks blurry.

The same happens with stars: their light crosses the Earth's air, which has warm and cold bubbles moving all the time. Those bubbles bend the light a tiny bit and the star seems to dance and twinkle.

The seeing is a number that says how much the star dances. It is measured in «arcseconds» (″), a very small unit of angle: 1″ is the size of a 1 cm coin seen from 2 km away.

The smaller the seeing, the sharper the sky and the better for observing.

Los <b>GOES</b> (Geostationary Operation:
NOAA's GOES (Geostationary Operational Environmental Satellites) orbit 35,786 km above the equator at the same speed as the Earth turns: from the ground they look still. GOES-East sits over longitude 75.2° W, almost above Colombia (GOES-16 until 4 April 2025 and GOES-19 since then). Its camera, the ABI (Advanced Baseline Imager), takes an image of the full disk of the Earth every 10 minutes in 16 channels: 6 of visible and near-infrared light, which reflect sunlight and only work in daytime, and 10 infrared ones that measure the brightness temperature (the temperature at which a black body would emit that radiation), day and night. The pixel is 2 km below the satellite (0.5–1 km in some visible channels) and a bit larger away from it.

Each channel «sees» at a different height: where the air is transparent at that wavelength, the satellite sees the ground or the cloud tops; where a gas (water vapor, CO₂, ozone) absorbs, it sees the layer of the atmosphere where that gas emits. Comparing channels gives information about several heights at once.

Qué es r. En cada cuadro el DIMM mide el: What r is. In each frame the DIMM measures the vector joining the two spots, and its motion is split into a longitudinal component (along the line joining the holes) and a transverse one (perpendicular). Pearson's correlation coefficient, r = Σ(xᵢ − x̄)(yᵢ − ȳ) / √[Σ(xᵢ − x̄)² · Σ(yᵢ − ȳ)²], goes from −1 to 1 and tells whether two motions tend to vary together (r > 0), in opposite directions (r < 0) or unrelated (r ≈ 0).

Si tomamos solo unos pocos cuadros al az:
If we take just a few frames at random, their mean changes every time. If we repeat that thousands of times, the means also form a bell (this is the central limit theorem).

The width of that bell of means is the standard error of the mean (formula below).

That's why we record thousands of frames: with 4 times more frames the error is cut in half; with 100 times more, to a tenth.

Tapamos el telescopio con una cartulina:
We cover the telescope with a piece of cardboard that has two little holes. That way the starlight comes in through two different paths and we see two spots instead of one.

If the telescope shakes (because of the wind or because someone touches it), both spots move together. But air turbulence affects each path differently, so the spots move closer together and farther apart from each other.

That's why we don't measure where the star is, but the distance between the two spots. That distance changes a little in every frame of the video, and the statistics of those changes tell us the seeing.

Un <b>dato atípico</b> está muy lejos de:
An outlier is very far from the rest. It can be real or a measurement error.

A true story: in the original program this project started from, 68 frames of the Altair video showed only one spot. The program paired them wrongly and produced false distances close to 0 px. With only 68 bad data points out of 8,484, the standard deviation almost doubled and the seeing came out worse than it really was.

TurbuLENS detects those frames and also applies a robust clipping: it discards the data that lie more than 5 «robust σ» from the median (it uses the MAD, which is not dragged by the extremes).

A measurement is a number we get by observing something. Here we measure the distance between the two spots of the star's image, in pixels (px).

Each frame of the video gives one data point. With a 2-minute video at 60 frames per second we have more than 8,000 data points of the same variable.

The data we have are a sample. The population would be all the possible measurements of that night. With statistics we use the sample to learn about the population.
